title: Differentially Private Statistical Inference for Rankings from Pairwise Comparisons
summary: Reliable inference for rankings of large language models based on human pairwise comparisons must preserve the privacy of individual preference records. To meet this need, we develop methods for score and rank inference under the Bradley-Terry model with edge differential privacy. For an objective-perturbed estimator, a new leave-one-out analysis establishes finite-sample bounds on Euclidean and entrywise estimation errors. For sufficiently dense comparison graphs, the error bounds extend to smaller privacy budgets, including regimes in which its privacy term dominates its statistical term. A uniform asymptotic expansion yields asymptotically valid confidence intervals for individual scores and pairwise score differences. To improve finite-sample performance, we account for both regularization bias and privacy-induced randomness by combining a plug-in ridge-bias correction with Gaussian-Laplace calibration. We further establish a bootstrap procedure for simultaneous rank inference, providing asymptotically valid confidence sets for individual ranks and tests of top-$K$ membership. When the comparison probability is public and known, all proposed inferential procedures require no additional privacy budget. We evaluate finite-sample performance through simulations and apply the proposed methods to rank large language models for creative writing.

title: Deceleration without identification: testing a power-law trend in Bitcoin prices under persistent noise
comment: 25 pages, 6 figures. Pre-registered protocol and forecasts: https://osf.io/2rdty. Replication package: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23218897
summary: Plotted against time since its first block on logarithmic axes, the price of Bitcoin lies close to a straight line, and a power law in time has been proposed as its long-run trend. A good fit is weak evidence: when deviations from a trend are as persistent as a random walk, regressions on time find trends and high $R^2$ where none exist. We first bound what fifteen years of weekly prices can reveal, then test only what is answerable. Using a few low-frequency averages, invariant to the noise scale and calibrated over a declared family of persistent deviations with a four-year cycle and declining volatility, we test constant drift in expected log price against an added log-age term. The procedure was fixed, validated and publicly hashed before it was applied once. Constant drift is rejected under this family at nominal 5%, and a log-age coefficient of 5.7, close to the published exponent, is not rejected. The rejection does not survive allowing persistence beyond a random walk, and a Gompertz curve with a ceiling fits about as well as the power law. Whether deviations revert to the trend cannot be decided. Registered forecasts for 2027-2030 will be scored by future prices.

title: How much can a human being lift? A Bayesian latent capability model for Olympic weightlifting
summary: Estimates of the limits of human performance are usually built on record books, on the premise that a record is the best an athlete could do. In Olympic weightlifting the premise fails, because the competitor declares the weight before each of three attempts per lift and only the heaviest successful attempt is recorded, so a record is a lower bound, chosen by the athlete, on a maximal capability never observed. We treat the maximal lift of each competitor on each competition day as a latent variable, of which every attempt is a trial and every declared weight a measurement. Its distribution at a given bodyweight follows an extreme value mixture model with an estimated threshold, and an athlete-specific random effect links the competitions of each athlete. The model is fitted to the 117,892 attempts of 5,040 athletes in 141 international competitions between 2017 and 2026. The upper tail of capability is bounded, with posterior probability above 0.999 for men, 0.96 for the women's snatch and 0.94 for the women's clean and jerk. At 110 kilograms of bodyweight the men's ceiling lies one to three per cent above the heaviest lifts, against twelve and sixteen per cent for women at 86 kilograms. The record book alone places the men's ceiling six and twelve kilograms higher, because the best lift of a day ending on a success overstates capability.
